column1: # Clear Bible's alignments the corpus reads (github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, under ClearBible/), one row per set, with
#   everything about a set that differs from the others: its files, how its words join the corpus's, where its numbers come
#   from, which of its defects' word lists it is read with, and what its links say of themselves. Ours, read from each set and
#   measured on the corpus; the reason says why. Edit a row and run forge build: stated-pairs reads the file for every pair
#   from, to     the translation the set is about and the witness it aligns it to, as the corpus slugs them
#   alignment    the records, under ClearBible/; target: one row per token of the translation, in the tokenisation the
#                records number (\N where the release ships none that fits); source: one row per word of the source edition
#   join         how the source edition's words become the witness's: letters (aligned inside the verse each text numbers
#                for itself) or edition (word against word, for an edition close to the witness)
#   numbering    where the numbers the records give the translation's words come from: tokenfile; retokenised (the
#                translation's own words, counted as the records count them); revised (a later revision of the token file than
#                the records were numbered over, checked against the glosses); redivided (a verse here and there counted over
#   edited       t where the records are numbered over the source edition as the team edited it verse by verse (ClearBibleSourceEdits)
#   and, also    where the set puts source words on the translation's word for "and" that the word after it renders: the
#                sources/words.tsv list (source clear-bible) of that word, and the list of the Strong numbers of the source
#                words that are not tagged conjunctions and can still be rendered by it; \N where the set does not (ClearBibleLinks.Shifted)
#   early        where the set puts a name, or a noun, verb or adjective, on the preposition or article before it and leaves
#                that word unnamed: the list of those prepositions and articles (ClearBibleLinks.Early, ClearBibleLinks.Slipped);
#   statement    what the set's links answer a reader with (link source): the team and the licence, not the path
#   reason       why the row is as it is

column12: Clear Bible Alignments WLCM-RV09-manual, BiblioNexus, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: The Reina-Valera 1909 against the Hebrew, hand-made, whole Old Testament. Its metadata names the target as identifier = "RV09" at ebible.org/find/details.php?id=spaRV1909, which is the file this corpus loads, and that identity was checked against the text rather than taken from the metadata: of the 31,082 verses both hold, 30,441 are word for word the same once accents and punctuation are folded, and the words that differ are that copy's own typographical slips — confudió, denlante, nostros. A different Reina-Valera would differ in thousands of verses rather than in 350 words.

column12: Clear Bible Alignments WLCM-LSG-manual, Biblica, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: The Segond of 1910 against the Hebrew, hand-made by Biblica's team, whole Old Testament. The release ships no list of its French words: the Old Testament token file is a header and nothing else, and the New Testament's does not match its own records — 7,475 of the 104,807 French words they name are a comma or a full stop in it, the way the Russian set's are. The records were numbered over the text divided at every elision, so that l’un is two words, with a hyphenated word kept whole and each mark of punctuation counted; the token file divides some elisions and not others. Counted that way over eBible's text, which has the same letters in 7,946 of the New Testament's 7,959 verses, 0.9% of the words the Old Testament's records name are punctuation, and a verse where any is has its records refused whole, since past that point every number in it is out. Of the records kept, a Hebrew proper name falls on a capitalised French word 98.7% of the time, where the Reina-Valera's own token file gives 97.3%. The set puts about two hundred Hebrew words on et where the next word renders them, as the Reina-Valera's does on y; in the New Testament the same shape is 36 records out of 5,713 on et, and those read as the translation's own choice.

column12: Clear Bible Alignments WLCM-AVD-manual, BiblioNexus, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: The Van Dyck against the Hebrew, hand-made by BiblioNexus, whole Old Testament. Its metadata points at the Digital Bible Library's fully vowelled Van Dyck rather than at eBible's, and says in a comment that nobody was sure it is the same version. It is: every word of both token files falls on a word of eBible's text, with a psalm's title — which the files number as a verse 0 — laid at the head of its first verse, and 408 of the two sets' 348,102 records name a Hebrew or Greek word this corpus could not place. One verse of the Old Testament's was counted over another division: in 1 Kings 13:23 הֵשִׁיב names the comma after أَرْجَعَهُ, אֲשֶׁר names أَرْجَعَهُ and the prophet takes ٱلَّذِي, each one word late.

column12: Clear Bible Alignments WLCM-IRVHin-manual, NLCI, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: The Indian Revised Version against the Hebrew, hand-made by NLCI, whole Old Testament. The set's own terms are CC BY 4.0 and the text's are CC BY-SA 4.0. A link names a Hindi word and a Hebrew or Greek one and holds no text of either, so it is a statement about the text and not an adaptation of it, and it carries the set's terms rather than the text's. The Old Testament set puts 376 Hebrew words on और where nothing names the word after it, as the Reina-Valera's does on y; in a sample of twelve, none is rendered by the और — seven are the object marker אֵת and the rest belong to the word after. The New Testament's has 13 of that shape and they are left alone.

column12: Clear Bible Alignments SBLGNT-JFA11-transfer, BiblioNexus, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, transferred from their Spanish Reina-Valera 1909 alignment, not made by hand
column13: The Almeida of 1911 against the Greek, New Testament only, and not made by hand: BiblioNexus transferred it from their hand-made alignment of the Spanish Reina-Valera 1909, and the set's own metadata says so — process = "transfer from Spanish RVR09" — while every one of its records says origin = "manual". The metadata is the statement about the set and is the one repeated on every link, so that nobody reads a transfer as somebody's reading of the Portuguese. Its target is Project Gutenberg's eBook 62383, the file this corpus loads, and its token file reads as that file does word for word, italics removed.

column12: Clear Bible Alignments WLC-YLT-manual, Clear Bible, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: Young's Literal Translation against the Hebrew, hand-made by Clear Bible's own team, whole Old Testament. The set calls its source WLC, and the release ships a WLC.tsv, but the records are numbered by the morpheme edition the other sets use: every source identifier they name is a row of WLCM.tsv, and 2,705 of them are no row of WLC.tsv. The two number a verse alike only until WLC.tsv writes two words as one (גֵ֣יא~בֶנ־הִנֹּ֔ם where the morpheme edition has גֵיא, בֶן and הִנֹּם, בֵֽית־אֵ֖ל where it has בֵית and אֵל) or a word as more morphemes (the article of בָּאֵשׁ); from there every identifier names a later word in one file than in the other. Read by WLC.tsv, Jeremiah 7:31's To burn stood on בְּנֵיהֶם and daughters on אֲשֶׁר; Genesis 12:8's Beth-El took the וַ after it. Its target is eBible's engylt, the file this corpus loads, and the token file numbers a psalm's title as verse 0 where that file prints it at the head of verse 1.

column12: Clear Bible Alignments SBLGNT-YLT-manual, Clear Bible, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: Young's Literal Translation against the Greek, hand-made by Clear Bible's team, whole New Testament. Young translated the Textus Receptus and the set is keyed to the SBLGNT, so a verse the critical text omits has no record, and a word only Young's Greek has is rendered by nothing. Except where the team edited the SBLGNT first, mostly toward the Nestle-Aland. In some 340 verses the records are numbered over the verse with a word added (Matthew 3:16's bracketed αὐτῷ after ἠνεῴχθησαν, Acts 3:6's ἔγειρε καί), taken out (Matthew 12:46's δέ, Revelation 5:4's ἐγώ) or moved (John 16:23's δώσει ὑμῖν, Galatians 1:3's ἡμῶν), and every number after it names a word one place out: read by SBLGNT.tsv, Matthew 3:16's the heavens stood on καί and he saw on πνεῦμα, and 367 identifiers in 266 verses name no word at all. No file in the release holds the edited text, so it is read back from the records (ClearBibleSourceEdits).

column12: Clear Bible Alignments SBLGNT-IRVBen-manual, NLCI, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand

column12: Clear Bible Alignments SBLGNT-OHCB-manual, BiblioNexus, github.com/Clear-Bible/Alignments, CC BY 4.0, made by hand
column13: Biblica's Open Hausa Contemporary Bible against the Greek, hand-made by BiblioNexus, whole New Testament. The release also ships a WLCM-OHCB-manual.json for the Old Testament, and it is this file byte for byte — the same 63,852 records, every one naming a Greek word — so there is no Hausa alignment to the Hebrew to load. In 26 verses a record names a mark of punctuation, and none of them is misnumbered: the team put a Greek word the Hausa does not render on the mark nearest its place, ἰδοὺ on the comma of Mark 3:32, ἐστιν on the full stop of Matthew 26:18, and every number after it names its word. Such a record places nothing, and the verse stands.
